title: Batch size, epochs, and reading a training curve properly

videos.script: Ten epochs sounds like an amount of training. On its own, it is not one. {{clocks}} An epoch is one pass over the training images. A step is one move of the weights. At a batch of thirty-two, one epoch on the digits is thirty-four steps. {{steps}} Train for ten epochs at a batch of one, and the network reaches almost ninety-seven per cent. Use the whole set as one batch, and it reaches forty-four. {{epochs}} Give both the same number of steps instead, and the big batch wins. It just does a thousand times the work. {{work}} A bigger batch wants a bigger learning rate, roughly in proportion. That rule holds for a while, and then it breaks. {{scaling}} The second half of the lesson is about reading the curve a run prints. Which line lags, how much is noise, and where to stop. {{curve}} Then four runs fail on purpose. A network too small, too few images, a rate too high, and labels shuffled by a bug. {{four}} Each one draws its own shape. By the end, you can tell them apart before you change anything. {{end}}
